The keyboard adjusts the suggestions to your typing. Nothing leaves your device

The keyboard keeps the words and the word pairs that you type in a private word list on this device. This makes the suggestions and glide typing better. The keyboard learns nothing in a password field, and nothing while incognito mode is on. You can delete the learned words below at any time.
Add words to the system dictionary
Share the learned words with the Android personal dictionary

The keyboard also saves the words that you type in the Android personal dictionary. Other keyboards and the spell checker of the system then know these words too. It is the same list that you can edit in System settings → Languages & input → Dictionary. This setting is off at the start: the keyboard has its own learning, and this setting writes outside the app. It obeys \"Learn from typing\" and incognito mode. When you turn it off, the words that are already in the list stay there.
Type a shortcut to get its full phrase as a suggestion

Each entry in the Android personal dictionary can have a shortcut. It is the same list in System settings → Languages & input → Dictionary. With this setting on, you type a shortcut, for example \"omw\", and its full phrase, \"on my way\", becomes the top suggestion. This setting is off at the start. The keyboard reads the list again when it next opens, so a shortcut that you just added shows after you change to a different app.
While this setting is on, the keyboard learns nothing from your typing and keeps no clipboard history. The words that it learned before stay as they are.
Turn incognito mode on by itself in private tabs and fields

An app can mark a text field as a field that the keyboard must not learn from. Chrome does this for every field in an incognito tab. Other browsers and password managers do the same on their private screens. While such a field has the focus, the keyboard turns incognito mode on for it, and the incognito badge shows next to the toolbar. When you leave the field, typing goes back to normal. The keyboard cannot detect an app that never sends this mark. This setting does not work for a private mode of that kind.
Include the keyboard in the Android backup and in the device-to-device transfer

This setting is off at the start. The keyboard copies nothing that it stores to Google Drive or to a new device. Turn it on, and the Android backup treats the keyboard like any other app. Your settings, themes, layouts, snippets, learned words, sticker packs, icon packs and plugins come back on a new device, or after you install the app again. The backup leaves out the voice models, the AI models, the downloaded word lists and the emoji keyword packs. The keyboard can download these again by itself, and the backup must stay inside the size limit of Android. The backup does include your saved API keys. Android makes a cloud backup only on a device that can encrypt it with your screen lock. Backup & restore in Settings is the other way, and it never uses Google. It saves the same data in a file that you move yourself.

Typing works fully on this device. The word lists, prediction, autocorrect, transliteration and emoji search are part of the app, and none of them needs a network connection. The app has no telemetry and no analytics. Only a tool uses the network, and only at the moment that you press it: translate, weather, web search, image search, GIFs, stickers, dictionary lookup and the AI tools. You can turn off each one of them on the Tools screen.
See what the keyboard can reach, and give or take back a permission

The keyboard works without all of these permissions. Each one unlocks one optional feature. Press a row to give the permission. Press a granted row to open the system settings, where you can take it back.
Dictate text with the voice input tool
Take a photo with the camera tool and send it into the chat
Suggest the names and the email addresses of your contacts while you type
The calendar tool lists the events of your day
Show your new screenshots in the clipboard
Save images from the keyboard to your gallery
Media controls on the keyboard, and one-time codes from your notifications
Show which app a clipboard entry was copied from
Keep the keyboard gestures while TalkBack is on
Only the network tools use it: translate, weather, search, GIFs, stickers, dictionary and the AI tools

Haptic feedback when you press a key

Android gives the permissions in the last group to every app at the install. An app cannot ask for them, and cannot give them back. You can take every other permission back at any time in the system settings. The feature that uses it then stops, and the rest of the keyboard keeps working.
A snippet is a piece of text that you use again and again, for example an address, an email sign-off or a standard reply. You insert a snippet from the snippet panel of the keyboard with one press.
any date format that you want

A variable expands at the moment that you insert the snippet, not when you save it. Because of this, {date} always gives the current date. {date:…} takes a pattern, for example {date:EEEE} or {date:dd/MM/yy}.
Expands by itself from the pattern: %1$s

A pattern lets one snippet take a different piece of text each time. Give the snippet the pattern ^hello (.+)$ and the text \"Hello, $1! Nice to meet you.\" Then type \"hello John\" and a space, and the keyboard writes \"Hello, John! Nice to meet you.\" Use $1 to $9 for each part in brackets, and ${1:upper}, ${1:lower}, ${1:title} or ${1:trim} to change one. One backspace puts back what you typed.
